title: Primary Key
description: Choose and enforce a primary identity, distinguish uniqueness from generation and ordering, and test single-column and composite SQL primary keys.
notes:
## The selected identity of a relation

A primary key is the candidate key selected as a relation's principal declared identifier. Its values identify tuples uniquely, and every key component must be nonmissing. In Student(student_id, student_name, programme), a declared primary key on student_id means that one identifier cannot belong to two stored student rows. The name and programme can repeat because they play different descriptive roles.

A table can have at most one PRIMARY KEY constraint, and that constraint can involve several attributes. Ordinary SQL definitions can omit a primary-key declaration, depending on engine and configuration rules, so it is inaccurate to say every possible SQL table necessarily declares exactly one. Good identity design and a particular product's permitted syntax are related but distinct questions.

## Uniqueness and nonmissing values work together

Uniqueness prevents two rows from claiming the same identifying value or combination. Nonmissing key components ensure the declared identity is definite. A primary key combines these obligations. It does not require the identifier to be an integer, positive, consecutive, or meaningful to users unless separate rules establish those properties. Text or composite identifiers can also be appropriate under the model.

A plain nullable UNIQUE column has a different absence policy. In MySQL, multiple NULLs can be allowed by a nullable unique constraint. If an alternate identity must be both unique and required, use a compatible nonmissing declaration as well. Do not infer a classical required identifier from the word UNIQUE alone, and do not assume other products implement optional uniqueness in precisely the same way.

## A composite primary key is one constraint

Enrollment can use student_id and course_id together when its fact grain is one enrollment per student-course pair. The combined values identify the enrollment. One student can appear in several pairs, and one course can appear with several students. A primary key on the pair is one constraint, not two independent primary keys.

Declaring each component separately as PRIMARY KEY is invalid as a way to request two primary keys. Declaring each separately UNIQUE would impose different, overly restrictive rules: a student could occur only once and a course could occur only once. State the combined identifying rule directly. Include valid repeated components in fixtures so the difference is observable rather than hidden by a one-row example.

## Choose the key from the fact grain

If the database records multiple attempts at one course, the student-course pair may no longer identify one tuple. A separate attempt identifier or an appropriate expanded combination is needed to distinguish occurrences. Adding a descriptive value such as score merely to avoid collisions can permit contradictory copies of the same intended attempt and conceal the underlying identity problem.

A student name is usually a poor primary identity because different students can share it and one student's name can change. An institutional number may be a candidate if policy guarantees its uniqueness and availability. An internal surrogate can be useful when business labels are mutable or inconvenient for references. The decision should follow explicit identity and lifecycle requirements rather than assuming the first column must be primary.

## Generated values are a separate feature

Declaring PRIMARY KEY does not by itself generate the next identifier. MySQL offers AUTO_INCREMENT for supported definitions, but generation and uniqueness are separate ideas. An ordinary INT PRIMARY KEY can require the caller to supply an acceptable identifier. A generated identifier can have gaps after rejected operations or other engine behaviour; it should not be treated as a guaranteed count of students.

Automatic generation also changes how some inputs are interpreted. In particular, inserting NULL into an auto-generated identity can request generation under the applicable product rules rather than serving as a simple test of prohibited missing identity. To test nonmissing primary-key enforcement directly, use a definition without that generation behaviour and isolate the intended error condition.

## Physical indexing is not logical row order

A database can use an index to enforce or access a primary key. Physical details depend on the storage engine; a logical key definition alone is not a universal claim about file layout across products. Nor does a fast key lookup guarantee every query using that table is fast. Predicates, result size, selected attributes, and available plans still matter.

A primary key also does not promise that SELECT output is sorted by that key. Request ORDER BY when an application needs deterministic presentation. The identifier can supply a useful tie-breaker because it distinguishes rows, but the ordering contract belongs to the query. An observed index traversal is not a substitute for the explicitly requested sort order.

## Changing referenced identities has consequences

Other relations can use foreign keys to refer to a primary identity. Changing a referenced value therefore requires understanding the configured referential actions and allowed transitions. An enforced rule may reject the change, or a supported cascading policy may coordinate it. It is misleading to say every such update silently creates orphans or every database automatically repairs all references.

Stable identifiers reduce unnecessary changes to referencing facts. A surrogate can often remain unchanged when a student's email changes, but it is not metaphysically immutable: systems can still require carefully managed identity migrations. Describe stability as a design objective and policy, not a guarantee that an artificial identifier can never need to change under any future circumstances.

## Add a primary key only to compatible data

A proposed key cannot be applied successfully to conflicting existing rows without a deliberate resolution. Audit repeated proposed identities and prohibited missing components first. A table may look correct when sampled while containing an unseen conflict elsewhere. A successful SELECT or application typecheck does not prove an ALTER TABLE operation would succeed on the complete intended dataset.

```sql
ALTER TABLE students
ADD PRIMARY KEY (student_id);
```

The statement expresses a schema requirement, not a data-cleanup algorithm. Do not delete arbitrary conflicting records or invent replacement identities merely to make it succeed. In an isolated exercise, fixtures can already satisfy the proposed rule. A real application change requires authorized migration planning, dependency review, and verification appropriate to the existing data and callers.

## Test key enforcement and permitted repetition

A focused test starts with two valid student identities sharing a name. It then attempts an existing identity with different descriptive values and expects rejection. A separate test attempts a prohibited missing identity. Different values outside the key must not make a duplicate identifying value acceptable. Otherwise the constraint is protecting a wider combination than the intended primary identity.

For a composite key, test several students on one course and one student on several courses. Then attempt the same complete pair with a changed score. The duplicate identity should still be rejected. Optional non-key attributes can remain NULL when allowed, so verify that primary-key enforcement does not accidentally turn every column into a required field or alter the meaning of missing scores.

## Explain exactly what was proved

An exercise can verify accepted rows, duplicate rejection, nonmissing key enforcement, and the resulting query output on its local engine. It cannot establish every foreign-key transition, authorization rule, or production migration property unless those paths were actually tested. Keep MariaDB compatibility execution distinct from exact MySQL or hosted-provider execution, and identify temporary-table scope where that is the chosen local mechanism.

For tied score reports, the unique identifier can resolve otherwise unspecified presentation ties. A dependable primary-key design selects a genuine minimal identity, preserves legitimate repeated descriptive values, and states how references and lifecycle changes are handled. Separate that identity from generation, display order, and performance assumptions. Then verify both permitted facts and targeted failures. These distinctions make the primary key a clear data contract rather than a vague label attached to whichever column happens to look important.

questions.question_text: What two constraints does declaring a column PRIMARY KEY enforce automatically?
options: UNIQUE and NOT NULL
CHECK and DEFAULT
FOREIGN KEY and CASCADE
INDEX and TRIGGER
questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY bundles uniqueness with a mandatory NOT NULL requirement.

questions.question_text: How many separate PRIMARY KEY constraints can one SQL table declare?
options: As many as needed
At most one, which may span several columns
Exactly two
Zero, unless UNIQUE is also declared
questions.explanation: A table may omit a primary-key declaration under ordinary supported definitions, but it cannot declare multiple separate primary keys.

questions.question_text: What is the key difference between PRIMARY KEY and a plain UNIQUE constraint?
options: There is no real difference
PRIMARY KEY additionally forbids NULL values, while plain UNIQUE still permits NULL
UNIQUE is enforced faster than PRIMARY KEY
PRIMARY KEY can only apply to text columns
questions.explanation: Both enforce uniqueness, but PRIMARY KEY also mandates NOT NULL — UNIQUE alone does not.

questions.question_text: In an SQL engine that indexes primary keys, what is the index’s role?
options: The column is encrypted
It supports key enforcement and access; actual query speed and storage details require engine-specific evidence
The column is automatically converted to text
All other columns become NOT NULL too
questions.explanation: Index support does not promise every query is faster or that results have an inherent order.

questions.question_text: Why is changing a primary key's values risky once other tables reference it via foreign keys?
options: It is never actually risky
Referencing facts depend on that identity, so rejection or coordinated changes depend on configured integrity rules
Foreign keys automatically update themselves with zero configuration in every engine
Primary keys cannot be referenced by foreign keys in the first place
questions.explanation: The update may be rejected or handled by supported configured actions; it does not necessarily create orphans.

questions.question_text: Why might a surrogate key be preferred as the primary key over a natural value like email?
options: Surrogate keys are always shorter to type
It can remain stable when mutable business labels change, reducing unnecessary reference changes
Natural keys are illegal as primary keys
There is no real reason; it's purely arbitrary
questions.explanation: Stability is a design advantage, not a universal guarantee that a surrogate can never change.

questions.question_text: Can a table have a composite primary key spanning two columns and still be considered to have 'one' primary key?
options: No, that would count as two primary keys
Yes — a composite primary key spanning multiple columns is still exactly one primary key constraint
Only if both columns are of the same data type
Composite primary keys are not allowed in SQL
questions.explanation: A composite primary key is one single constraint that happens to involve more than one column.

questions.question_text: What happens if you try to declare PRIMARY KEY on two different columns of the same table separately?
options: The table gets two independent primary keys
This is a schema error — a table can only have one PRIMARY KEY constraint (use a composite key if multiple columns are needed together)
The first declaration silently wins with no error
SQL automatically merges them into a UNIQUE constraint instead
questions.explanation: You cannot have two separate PRIMARY KEY constraints on one table; a genuinely multi-column key must be declared as one composite PRIMARY KEY.

questions.question_text: Does PRIMARY KEY alone generate the next integer identifier?
options: Yes; all keys auto-increment
No; generation requires a separate supported feature
Only when sorted
Only for an empty table
questions.explanation: Identity enforcement and value generation are distinct.

questions.question_text: Does a primary key promise SELECT output order?
options: Yes; every query is key-sorted
Only text keys lack order
No; request ORDER BY for the presentation contract
Only composite keys require sorting
questions.explanation: Logical identity does not imply a result ordering guarantee.

questions.question_text: Why can a repeated name be valid under a student_id primary key?
options: All names are automatically unique
The key only applies to the first row
Name is descriptive and different identities can share it
Repeated names disable the primary key
questions.explanation: The constraint concerns the declared identity attributes.

questions.question_text: What should happen to the same primary identifier with a different name?
options: It must become a second valid identity
It changes the key definition
It is always silently merged
It should still violate the primary uniqueness rule
questions.explanation: Changing non-key values does not create a different key identity.

questions.question_text: Why is NULL insertion into an auto-generated identifier not a simple missing-key rejection test?
options: It may request generation under the engine’s rules
NULL always means zero
Generated keys have no constraints
Every test must use a name instead
questions.explanation: Generation changes the semantics of supplied values.

questions.question_text: Why should student_id and course_id not each be separately UNIQUE for an ordinary many-to-many enrollment?
options: It would permit duplicate pairs
That would prohibit legitimate repeated individual components
It would remove every type
It would make names mandatory
questions.explanation: The combined pair, not each component alone, identifies the enrollment.

questions.question_text: Does adding a key declaration resolve conflicting existing rows automatically?
options: Yes; it always deletes conflicts
Yes; it invents student identities
No; compatible data or an authorized resolution is needed
Only when a SELECT succeeds
questions.explanation: The constraint is not a data-cleanup policy.

questions.question_text: Why can an artificial identifier be useful when email changes?
options: It proves email ownership
It guarantees no business rule is needed
It prevents all future migrations
It can preserve the referenced identity independently of that label
questions.explanation: Stable internal identity can decouple references from mutable business fields.

questions.question_text: What must be inspected before changing a referenced primary value?
options: Foreign-key definitions and configured transition behaviour
Only the table title
Only the first displayed row
Only column label length
questions.explanation: References constrain what identity changes are allowed.

questions.question_text: Does a primary key make every non-key attribute NOT NULL?
options: Yes; every column becomes required
No; non-key nullability follows its own declaration
Only names become required
Only scores become required
questions.explanation: Key-component requirements do not automatically apply to all attributes.

questions.question_text: What is needed if repeated course attempts are separate facts?
options: Always a key on score alone
Only a name change
An identity that distinguishes the intended occurrences
Removing every uniqueness rule
questions.explanation: The primary identity must match the fact grain.

questions.question_text: Which claim is supported by isolated key-enforcement tests?
options: Production migration success
Every provider’s referential actions
All application authorization paths
The exercised key behaviour on the recorded local engine
questions.explanation: Evidence is limited to the actual exercised boundary.

coding_problems.title: Add and verify one student primary identity
coding_problems.task: Add PRIMARY KEY(student_id) to students, then return student_id and student_name. The definition has no automatic identifier generation. Repeated names remain allowed.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add the primary key and return student identities and names.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT NULL, student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
constraints: Initial identifiers are unique and nonmissing.
edge_cases: A duplicate identifier with a different name must fail.
A missing identifier must fail after key creation.
hints: ALTER TABLE can add the primary constraint.
A name is not part of this identity.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE students ADD PRIMARY KEY (student_id);
SELECT student_id, student_name FROM students ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The primary-key declaration establishes uniqueness and required identity values while permitting descriptive name repetition.

coding_problems.title: Add one composite enrollment primary key
coding_problems.task: Add one PRIMARY KEY(student_id, course_id) to enrollments. Return student_id, course_id and optional score. Keep missing non-key scores unchanged. The contract permits one enrollment per pair.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add the combined primary key, then return enrollment facts.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INT NULL, course_id INT NULL, score INT NULL);
constraints: Initial identity pairs are unique and nonmissing.
This local exercise does not establish parent existence or referential actions.
edge_cases: Individual key components can repeat in different pairs.
The non-key score can remain NULL.
hints: Use a single PRIMARY KEY clause listing both attributes.
Do not include score in the key.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id);
SELECT student_id, course_id, score FROM enrollments ORDER BY student_id, course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The one composite identity allows valid many-to-many pairs. Required key components do not make the optional score mandatory.

options: As many as needed
Exactly one (though it may span multiple columns)
Exactly two
Zero, unless UNIQUE is also declared
original_questions.explanation: A table has exactly one primary key; it can be composite (multi-column) but there is still only one.

original_questions.question_text: What is the key difference between PRIMARY KEY and a plain UNIQUE constraint?

original_questions.question_text: What commonly happens automatically when a column is declared PRIMARY KEY?
options: The column is encrypted
The engine typically creates an index on it, speeding up lookups by that key
The column is automatically converted to text
All other columns become NOT NULL too
original_questions.explanation: Most engines auto-index the primary key since it's the most common lookup path — a helpful side effect, not something manually configured.

original_questions.question_text: Why is changing a primary key's values risky once other tables reference it via foreign keys?
options: It is never actually risky
Every referencing row's foreign key value would become invalid/orphaned unless carefully coordinated
Foreign keys automatically update themselves with zero configuration in every engine
Primary keys cannot be referenced by foreign keys in the first place
original_questions.explanation: Referencing rows depend on the primary key's exact value; changing it breaks that link unless a cascading update is explicitly set up.

original_questions.question_text: Why might a surrogate key be preferred as the primary key over a natural value like email?
options: Surrogate keys are always shorter to type
A surrogate key's value never needs to change for business reasons, making it a more stable long-term identifier
Natural keys are illegal as primary keys
There is no real reason; it's purely arbitrary
original_questions.explanation: A natural value can change (e.g. a person changes their email); a surrogate key's value has no business meaning and so never needs to change.
